questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which of the following physical quantities is a fundamental (base) SI quantity?
questions.Explanation: The seven SI base quantities are length (m), mass (kg), time (s), electric current (A), thermodynamic temperature (K), luminous intensity (cd), and amount of substance (mol).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which of the following instruments is most suitable for measuring the internal and external diameter of a narrow glass test tube accurately?
questions.Explanation: Vernier calipers feature inside jaws for internal diameters, outside jaws for external diameters, and a depth probe, with precision of 0.01 cm (0.1 mm).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A micrometer screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular thimble. What is the least count (smallest readable division) of the instrument?
questions.Explanation: Least count = Pitch / Number of divisions = 0.5 mm / 50 = 0.01 mm (0.001 cm).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What is the dimension of Force in terms of fundamental dimensions [M], [L], and [T]?
questions.Explanation: Force = mass × acceleration = [M] × [L T⁻²] = [M L T⁻²].

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What is the dimension of Pressure?
questions.Explanation: Pressure = Force / Area = [M L T⁻²] / [L²] = [M L⁻¹ T⁻²].

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which of the following pairs of physical quantities share the exact same dimensions?
questions.Explanation: Work (Force × distance) and Torque (Force × perpendicular distance) both have the dimension [M L² T⁻²] and SI unit N·m (or Joule for work).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The period T of a simple pendulum is given by T = 2π√(L/g). Which formula correctly relates the dimension of acceleration due to gravity [g]?
questions.Explanation: Squaring gives T² = 4π²(L/g) → g = 4π²L/T². In dimensions: [g] = [L] / [T]² = [L T⁻²].

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: If a micrometer screw gauge reads 3.5 mm on the main sleeve scale and the 24th thimble division coincides with the datum line (pitch = 0.5 mm, 50 divisions), what is the total reading?
questions.Explanation: Total reading = Main scale + (thimble division × least count) = 3.5 mm + (24 × 0.01 mm) = 3.5 + 0.24 = 3.74 mm.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A zero error on a vernier caliper or micrometer screw gauge is classified as a
questions.OptionA: systematic error that can be eliminated by calibration or zero correction
questions.OptionC: parallax error due to incorrect eye angle
questions.Option_a: systematic error that can be eliminated by calibration or zero correction
questions.Option_c: parallax error due to incorrect eye angle
questions.Explanation: Zero error is a constant instrument-dependent systematic error corrected by subtracting or adding the zero offset from all measured readings.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What is the dimension of Universal Gravitational Constant (G) in Newton's law F = G·m1·m2 / r²?
questions.Explanation: G = F·r² / (m1·m2) = ([M L T⁻²] × [L²]) / [M²] = [M L³ T⁻²] / [M²] = [M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²].

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Parallax error when reading a liquid meniscus in a graduated cylinder is avoided by
questions.OptionA: looking down from above the cylinder
questions.OptionC: positioning the eye horizontally level with the bottom of the curved meniscus
questions.OptionD: measuring from the top edges of the meniscus curve
questions.Option_a: looking down from above the cylinder
questions.Option_c: positioning the eye horizontally level with the bottom of the curved meniscus
questions.Option_d: measuring from the top edges of the meniscus curve
questions.Explanation: Viewing horizontally level with the lowest point of a concave water meniscus eliminates parallax error.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which of the following represents an SI derived unit expressed in fundamental base units?
questions.Explanation: Work = Force × distance = (kg·m·s⁻²) × m = kg·m²·s⁻² = 1 Joule.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The dimension of impulse of a force is identical to the dimension of
questions.Explanation: Impulse = Force × time = [M L T⁻²] × [T] = [M L T⁻¹], which is identically the dimension of linear momentum (mass × velocity).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which of the following physical quantities is a vector quantity?
questions.Explanation: Vectors possess both magnitude and spatial direction; displacement has direction, whereas distance, mass, and speed are scalars.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which of the following groups consists exclusively of vector quantities?
questions.OptionC: Velocity, Acceleration, Weight, and Electric field intensity
questions.OptionD: Work, Power, Electric current, and Voltage
questions.Option_c: Velocity, Acceleration, Weight, and Electric field intensity
questions.Option_d: Work, Power, Electric current, and Voltage
questions.Explanation: Velocity, acceleration, weight (gravitational force), and electric field intensity are all vectors possessing magnitude and direction.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Two forces of magnitudes 3 N and 4 N act concurrently on a particle at right angles (90°) to each other. What is the magnitude of their resultant force?

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What is the maximum and minimum resultant force that can be obtained from two forces of 10 N and 6 N acting on a body?
questions.OptionA: Maximum = 16 N (in same direction), Minimum = 4 N (in opposite directions)
questions.Option_a: Maximum = 16 N (in same direction), Minimum = 4 N (in opposite directions)
questions.Explanation: Maximum resultant occurs at θ = 0° (10 + 6 = 16 N); minimum resultant occurs at θ = 180° (10 - 6 = 4 N).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A force of 50 N acts at an angle of 60° to the horizontal ground. What is the magnitude of its horizontal component?

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A force of 100 N acts at an angle of 30° to the horizontal. What is its vertical component?

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Three coplanar forces acting at a point are in equilibrium. According to Lami's theorem, each force is proportional to the
questions.OptionA: cosine of the angle between the other two forces
questions.OptionB: tangent of the angle opposite to it
questions.OptionC: square of the distance from the point
questions.OptionD: sine of the angle between the other two forces
questions.Option_a: cosine of the angle between the other two forces
questions.Option_b: tangent of the angle opposite to it
questions.Option_c: square of the distance from the point
questions.Option_d: sine of the angle between the other two forces
questions.Explanation: Lami's Theorem: P / sin(α) = Q / sin(β) = R / sin(γ) for three coplanar concurrent forces in equilibrium.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: An aeroplane flies due East with an airspeed of 120 km/h, while a wind blows due North at 50 km/h. What is the ground speed of the aeroplane?
questions.Explanation: Perpendicular vectors: v_resultant = √(120² + 50²) = √(14400 + 2500) = √16900 = 130 km/h.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: If two forces of equal magnitude F act on a particle at an angle of 120° to each other, what is the magnitude of their resultant force?

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The equilibrant of a system of forces is defined as the single force that
questions.OptionA: is equal in magnitude and acts in the exact same direction as the resultant
questions.OptionB: causes the body to accelerate at 9.8 m/s²
questions.OptionC: balances the resultant force, having the same magnitude but acting in the directly opposite direction
questions.OptionD: multiplies the angular velocity of the body
questions.Option_a: is equal in magnitude and acts in the exact same direction as the resultant
questions.Option_b: causes the body to accelerate at 9.8 m/s²
questions.Option_c: balances the resultant force, having the same magnitude but acting in the directly opposite direction
questions.Option_d: multiplies the angular velocity of the body

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A boat heads directly across a river of width 80 m at 4 m/s while the river current flows downstream at 3 m/s. How long does the boat take to cross the river?
questions.Explanation: The across-river velocity component is 4 m/s. Time to cross = distance across / velocity across = 80 m / 4 m/s = 20 s.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which of the following mathematical operations between two vectors A and B produces a scalar quantity?
questions.OptionB: Vector (cross) product: A × B = |A||B| sin(θ) n̂
questions.Option_b: Vector (cross) product: A × B = |A||B| sin(θ) n̂
questions.Explanation: The dot product A·B yields a scalar (e.g., Work = F·s = |F||s| cos θ).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Triangle Law of Vectors states that if two vectors acting concurrently on a point are represented in magnitude and direction by two sides of a triangle taken in order, their resultant is represented by
questions.OptionA: the hypotenuse divided by the base
questions.OptionB: the third closing side of the triangle taken in the reverse order
questions.Option_a: the hypotenuse divided by the base
questions.Option_b: the third closing side of the triangle taken in the reverse order
questions.Explanation: The triangle law states that the closing third side taken in reverse direction represents the resultant vector in magnitude and direction.

questions.Question: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to a speed of 20 m/s in 5 seconds. What is its acceleration?

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A train moving at an initial velocity of 30 m/s decelerates uniformly to rest in 10 seconds. What total distance does it cover during this braking period?

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: In a velocity-time graph, what physical quantity is represented by the area under the curve?
questions.Explanation: Area under a velocity-time graph equals the integral ∫ v dt, which gives total displacement.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: In a displacement-time graph, what physical quantity is represented by the slope (gradient) of the line?
questions.Explanation: Slope = Δs / Δt = velocity. For a velocity-time graph, slope gives acceleration.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A stone is dropped from the top of a cliff and hits the ground after 4.0 seconds. What is the height of the cliff? (Take g = 10 m/s²)

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A ball is projected vertically upward with an initial velocity of 30 m/s. What is the maximum height reached? (Take g = 10 m/s²)
questions.Explanation: At max height v = 0. v² = u² - 2gh → 0 = 30² - 2(10)h → 20h = 900 → h = 45 m.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A projectile is launched from ground level with initial velocity u at an angle θ to the horizontal. Which component of velocity remains constant throughout the flight, assuming air resistance is negligible?
questions.Explanation: Gravity acts purely downwards; with no horizontal force/drag, horizontal velocity ux = u cos θ remains strictly constant.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The maximum horizontal range R of a projectile on level ground is achieved when the angle of projection θ is
questions.Explanation: Range R = (u² sin 2θ) / g. R is maximized when sin(2θ) = 1 → 2θ = 90° → θ = 45°.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A projectile launched at 30° has the same horizontal range as another projectile launched with the same initial speed at an angle of
questions.Explanation: Projectiles launched at complementary angles (θ and 90° - θ) have identical horizontal ranges because sin(2θ) = sin(180° - 2θ).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A bullet is fired horizontally from a rifle at a height of 5 m above level ground with an initial speed of 200 m/s. How long does it take to hit the ground? (Take g = 10 m/s²)
questions.Explanation: Vertical motion is independent of horizontal speed: initial vertical velocity uy = 0. h = 1/2 gt² → 5 = 1/2 (10) t² → 5 = 5t² → t = 1.0 s.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What is the maximum height H reached by a projectile launched with speed u at angle θ to the horizontal?
questions.Explanation: At apex vy = 0: vy² = uy² - 2gH → 0 = (u sin θ)² - 2gH → H = u² sin² θ / (2g).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The time of flight T for a projectile launched at angle θ from level ground and landing at the same level is given by
questions.Explanation: Time to reach maximum height t = (u sin θ) / g. Total time of flight T = 2t = (2u sin θ) / g.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A body moving with uniform velocity has an acceleration equal to
questions.Explanation: Uniform velocity means constant magnitude and direction; velocity does not change with time, so acceleration a = dv/dt = 0.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Newton Laws of Motion, Momentum, and Friction
questions.Question: Newton's First Law of Motion states that an object will remain at rest or continue in a state of uniform motion in a straight line unless
questions.OptionA: its mass is reduced to zero
questions.OptionC: it collides with a photon of light
questions.OptionD: acted upon by an unbalanced external resultant force
questions.Option_a: its mass is reduced to zero
questions.Option_c: it collides with a photon of light
questions.Option_d: acted upon by an unbalanced external resultant force
questions.Explanation: Newton's first law (law of inertia) asserts that a body maintains constant velocity unless compelled to change by a net external force.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Newton Laws of Motion, Momentum, and Friction
questions.Question: Inertia is the inherent property of a body to resist changes in its state of rest or uniform motion. It is quantitatively measured by the body's
questions.Explanation: Mass is the quantitative measure of inertia; a body with greater mass has greater resistance to acceleration.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Newton Laws of Motion, Momentum, and Friction
questions.Question: Newton's Second Law of Motion states that the rate of change of momentum of a body is
questions.OptionB: directly proportional to the applied force and acts in the direction of the force (F = ma)
questions.OptionC: equal to the kinetic energy produced
questions.OptionD: independent of the time of force action
questions.Option_b: directly proportional to the applied force and acts in the direction of the force (F = ma)
questions.Option_c: equal to the kinetic energy produced
questions.Option_d: independent of the time of force action
questions.Explanation: Newton's 2nd Law: F = dp/dt = d(mv)/dt = m(dv/dt) = ma (for constant mass m).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Newton Laws of Motion, Momentum, and Friction
questions.Question: What net force is required to accelerate a 1200 kg car at a rate of 2.5 m/s²?

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.Question: Newton's Third Law of Motion states that for every action force, there is an
questions.OptionB: equal reaction force acting on the exact same body
questions.OptionD: equal and opposite reaction force acting on different bodies
questions.Option_b: equal reaction force acting on the exact same body
questions.Option_d: equal and opposite reaction force acting on different bodies
questions.Explanation: Action and reaction forces are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, simultaneous, and act on two different interacting bodies.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Newton Laws of Motion, Momentum, and Friction
questions.Question: The principle of conservation of linear momentum states that the total momentum of an isolated system remains constant provided
questions.OptionA: no net external resultant force acts on the system
questions.Option_a: no net external resultant force acts on the system
questions.Explanation: Conservation of momentum: In a closed, isolated system where ΣF_ext = 0, total initial momentum equals total final momentum.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Newton Laws of Motion, Momentum, and Friction
questions.Question: A ball of mass 2 kg moving at 6 m/s collides with and sticks to a stationary ball of mass 4 kg. What is their common velocity after collision?
questions.Explanation: Inelastic collision: m1u1 + m2u2 = (m1 + m2)v → (2 × 6) + (4 × 0) = (2 + 4)v → 12 = 6v → v = 2 m/s.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Newton Laws of Motion, Momentum, and Friction
questions.Question: An elastic collision differs from an inelastic collision because in an elastic collision,
questions.OptionA: only linear momentum is conserved, while kinetic energy is lost as heat
questions.OptionB: the colliding bodies stick together permanently
questions.OptionC: both linear momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved
questions.OptionD: kinetic energy increases after the collision
questions.Option_a: only linear momentum is conserved, while kinetic energy is lost as heat
questions.Option_b: the colliding bodies stick together permanently
questions.Option_c: both linear momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved
questions.Option_d: kinetic energy increases after the collision
questions.Explanation: In perfectly elastic collisions, both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. In inelastic collisions, kinetic energy is partially converted to heat/deformation.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Newton Laws of Motion, Momentum, and Friction
questions.Question: Impulse is defined as the product of force and time (F · Δt). It is equal to the
questions.OptionB: rate of change of kinetic energy
questions.OptionD: change in momentum of the body (Δp = mv - mu)
questions.Option_b: rate of change of kinetic energy
questions.Option_d: change in momentum of the body (Δp = mv - mu)
questions.Explanation: Impulse-momentum theorem: Impulse J = F · Δt = m·v - m·u = Δp.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Newton Laws of Motion, Momentum, and Friction
questions.Question: A force of 20 N acts on a body of mass 5 kg for 3 seconds. If the body was initially at rest, what is its final momentum?
questions.Explanation: Impulse = Change in momentum = F × t = 20 N × 3 s = 60 N·s = 60 kg·m/s. Initial momentum was 0, so final momentum is 60 kg·m/s.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Newton Laws of Motion, Momentum, and Friction
questions.Question: Limiting friction (Fs) is the maximum static friction that must be overcome to start moving a body. It is related to the normal reaction (R) by
questions.Explanation: The law of static friction gives Fs = μs · R, where μs is the coefficient of static friction and R is the normal reaction force.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Newton Laws of Motion, Momentum, and Friction
questions.Question: A wooden block of mass 10 kg rests on a horizontal table. If the coefficient of static friction is 0.4, what minimum horizontal force is required to start the block moving? (Take g = 10 m/s²)
questions.Explanation: Normal reaction R = mg = 10 × 10 = 100 N. Fs = μs · R = 0.4 × 100 N = 40 N.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Newton Laws of Motion, Momentum, and Friction
questions.Question: The angle of friction (λ) on a rough horizontal plane is related to the coefficient of static friction (μ) by the equation
questions.Explanation: The angle between the resultant contact force and the normal reaction at limiting equilibrium satisfies tan(λ) = Fs/R = μ.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Work, Energy, Power, and Simple Machines
questions.Question: Work is done when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force. Its SI unit is the
questions.Explanation: Work = Force × displacement = 1 N × 1 m = 1 Joule (J).

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.Question: A 5 kg stone is lifted to a height of 12 m above the ground. What is its gravitational potential energy relative to the ground? (Take g = 10 m/s²)
questions.Explanation: PE = m g h = 5 kg × 10 m/s² × 12 m = 600 J.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Work, Energy, Power, and Simple Machines
questions.Question: Power is defined as the rate of doing work or rate of energy transfer. Its SI unit is the
questions.Explanation: Power = Work / time = Joules per second = Watts (W).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Work, Energy, Power, and Simple Machines
questions.Question: The mechanical advantage (MA) of a simple machine is defined as the ratio of
questions.OptionB: Distance moved by effort to distance moved by load
questions.Option_b: Distance moved by effort to distance moved by load
questions.Explanation: Mechanical advantage: MA = Load / Effort.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Work, Energy, Power, and Simple Machines
questions.Question: The velocity ratio (VR) of a machine is defined as the ratio of the
questions.OptionA: distance moved by the effort to the distance moved by the load in the same time
questions.OptionD: weight of the machine to the load
questions.Option_a: distance moved by the effort to the distance moved by the load in the same time
questions.Option_d: weight of the machine to the load
questions.Explanation: Velocity ratio: VR = (Distance moved by Effort) / (Distance moved by Load). VR is independent of friction.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Work, Energy, Power, and Simple Machines
questions.Question: The efficiency (η) of a simple machine is related to its mechanical advantage (MA) and velocity ratio (VR) by the formula
questions.Explanation: Efficiency = (Work output / Work input) = (Load × d_load) / (Effort × d_effort) = MA / VR × 100%.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Work, Energy, Power, and Simple Machines
questions.Question: A machine with a velocity ratio of 5 requires an effort of 250 N to lift a load of 1000 N. What is the efficiency of the machine?
questions.Explanation: MA = Load / Effort = 1000 / 250 = 4. Efficiency = (MA / VR) × 100% = (4 / 5) × 100% = 80%.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Work, Energy, Power, and Simple Machines
questions.Question: In an inclined plane of length L and height h making an angle θ with the horizontal, the velocity ratio (VR) is given by
questions.Explanation: VR = Effort distance / Load distance = L / h = 1 / sin(θ).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Work, Energy, Power, and Simple Machines
questions.Question: Why can the efficiency of a real practical machine never exceed or equal 100%?
questions.OptionA: Part of the work input is always lost in overcoming internal friction and moving machine parts
questions.OptionB: Velocity ratio drops to zero during operation
questions.OptionC: The load becomes heavier than the effort
questions.OptionD: The acceleration due to gravity increases with speed
questions.Option_a: Part of the work input is always lost in overcoming internal friction and moving machine parts
questions.Option_b: Velocity ratio drops to zero during operation
questions.Option_c: The load becomes heavier than the effort
questions.Option_d: The acceleration due to gravity increases with speed
questions.Explanation: Friction between moving parts and moving the machine's own components dissipate energy as heat, ensuring efficiency < 100%.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: An object moving in a circle of radius r with constant speed v experiences a centripetal acceleration directed toward the
questions.OptionA: tangent to the circle in the direction of motion
questions.OptionB: center of the circular path, with magnitude a = v² / r
questions.OptionD: perpendicular to the plane of the circle
questions.Option_a: tangent to the circle in the direction of motion
questions.Option_b: center of the circular path, with magnitude a = v² / r
questions.Option_d: perpendicular to the plane of the circle
questions.Explanation: Centripetal acceleration continuously redirects velocity toward the center of the circular curvature: a_c = v² / r = ω²r.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The centripetal force required to keep a body of mass m moving in a circular path of radius r with linear speed v is given by
questions.Explanation: From Newton's second law: Fc = m · a_c = m v² / r = m ω² r.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A stone of mass 0.5 kg tied to a string of length 2 m rotates in a horizontal circle at a constant speed of 4 m/s. What is the tension in the string?
questions.Explanation: Tension provides centripetal force: T = m v² / r = (0.5 × 4²) / 2 = (0.5 × 16) / 2 = 8 / 2 = 4 N.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Angular velocity (ω) in radians per second is related to linear velocity (v) and radius (r) by the equation
questions.Explanation: Linear speed v along the arc is related to angular speed ω by v = ω r (where ω is in rad/s).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation states that the gravitational attractive force between two point masses m1 and m2 separated by distance r is
questions.Explanation: Newton's gravitation law: F = G m1 m2 / r², inversely proportional to the square of the distance.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: If the distance between two spherical masses is doubled, the gravitational force of attraction between them becomes
questions.Explanation: Inverse-square law: F ∝ 1/r². If r doubles (2r), F becomes 1/(2)² = 1/4 of the original force.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The acceleration due to gravity (g) at the surface of a spherical planet of mass M and radius R is given by
questions.Explanation: Equating weight mg to gravitational force G M m / R² yields g = G M / R².

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: How does acceleration due to gravity (g) vary as an object is moved from the Earth's equator to the North Pole?
questions.OptionA: It increases slightly because the Earth is an oblate spheroid, flatter at the poles (smaller radius R)
questions.OptionB: It decreases to zero at the pole
questions.OptionC: It remains completely constant everywhere on Earth
questions.OptionD: It drops by half at the pole
questions.Option_a: It increases slightly because the Earth is an oblate spheroid, flatter at the poles (smaller radius R)
questions.Option_b: It decreases to zero at the pole
questions.Option_c: It remains completely constant everywhere on Earth
questions.Option_d: It drops by half at the pole
questions.Explanation: The polar radius is ~21 km shorter than the equatorial radius; by g = GM/R², smaller radius yields higher g (~9.83 m/s² vs 9.78 m/s²).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The escape velocity (ve) from the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R is the minimum speed needed to escape its gravitational pull, given by
questions.Explanation: Equating initial kinetic energy 1/2 m ve² to gravitational potential energy GMm/R gives ve = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR) (~11.2 km/s on Earth).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The orbital velocity (v_orb) of an artificial satellite orbiting close to the surface of the Earth is given by
questions.Explanation: Centripetal force m v² / R = m g → v = √(g R) (~7.9 km/s on Earth).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A geostationary (geosynchronous) satellite appears stationary above a fixed point on Earth's equator because its orbital period is exactly
questions.OptionA: 12 hours, orbiting from North to South
questions.OptionD: 24 hours, orbiting from West to East
questions.Option_a: 12 hours, orbiting from North to South
questions.Option_d: 24 hours, orbiting from West to East
questions.Explanation: A geostationary satellite orbits in the equatorial plane with an orbital period of 24 hours, matching Earth's rotational period.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Kepler's Third Law of Planetary Motion states that the square of the orbital period (T) of a planet is directly proportional to the
questions.OptionA: cube of the semi-major axis (radius) of its orbit: T² ∝ r³
questions.OptionB: square of the radius: T² ∝ r²
questions.OptionD: cube root of the solar mass
questions.Option_a: cube of the semi-major axis (radius) of its orbit: T² ∝ r³
questions.Option_b: square of the radius: T² ∝ r²
questions.Option_d: cube root of the solar mass
questions.Explanation: Kepler's harmonic law: T² / r³ = constant for all bodies orbiting the same central mass.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: An astronaut in an orbiting spacecraft feels weightless because
questions.OptionB: both the astronaut and spacecraft are in a state of free fall toward Earth with the same gravitational acceleration
questions.OptionC: the spacecraft has escaped Earth's gravitational pull completely
questions.OptionD: the atmosphere shields the astronaut from gravity
questions.Option_b: both the astronaut and spacecraft are in a state of free fall toward Earth with the same gravitational acceleration
questions.Option_c: the spacecraft has escaped Earth's gravitational pull completely
questions.Option_d: the atmosphere shields the astronaut from gravity
questions.Explanation: Weightlessness in orbit is apparent: gravity is ~90% of surface value, but both vessel and astronaut fall freely together, so normal reaction R = 0.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The pressure P exerted at a depth h in a liquid of density ρ under gravity g is given by the hydrostatic formula
questions.Explanation: Liquid pressure: P = Force / Area = (Volume × ρ × g) / Area = (A h ρ g) / A = h ρ g.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What is the hydrostatic pressure at a depth of 5 m in a freshwater swimming pool? (Density of water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²)
questions.Explanation: P = h ρ g = 5 m × 1000 kg/m³ × 10 m/s² = 50,000 N/m² = 50 kPa.

questions.Topic: Gas Laws and Kinetic Theory of Gases
questions.Question: An air bubble of volume 2.0 cm^3 at the bottom of a lake 20 m deep rises to the surface. If surface atmospheric pressure is 10 m of water and temperature is constant, what is its volume at the surface?
questions.Explanation: Pressure at bottom P1 = h_water + H_atm = 20 m + 10 m = 30 m of water. Surface pressure P2 = 10 m of water. P1 * V1 = P2 * V2 => 30 * 2.0 = 10 * V2 => V2 = 60 / 10 = 6.0 cm^3.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Gas Laws and Kinetic Theory of Gases
questions.Question: What is the general gas equation for an ideal gas?
questions.Explanation: Combining Boyle's and Charles's laws gives the ideal gas relationship PV/T = constant, or (P1 * V1) / T1 = (P2 * V2) / T2.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Gas Laws and Kinetic Theory of Gases
questions.Question: What happens to the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) speed of ideal gas molecules if the absolute temperature is increased fourfold?
questions.Explanation: The r.m.s. velocity c_rms = sqrt(3 R T / M). Since c_rms is proportional to sqrt(T), quadrupling T multiplies c_rms by sqrt(4) = 2.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Gas Laws and Kinetic Theory of Gases
questions.Question: Standard temperature and pressure (S.T.P.) are defined respectively as:
questions.Explanation: S.T.P. standard conditions in physics correspond to 0 °C (273.15 K) and 1 atmosphere of pressure (760 mmHg or 1.013 x 10^5 Pa).

questions.OptionD: Directly proportional to its density at constant pressure

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which mechanism of heat transfer does NOT require any material medium for propagation?
questions.Explanation: Thermal radiation transfers energy via electromagnetic waves (chiefly infrared) and travels freely through a perfect vacuum at the speed of light.

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.OptionA: Metals possess a high density of free (delocalized) electrons that transfer kinetic energy rapidly

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which surface finish is the best emitter and the best absorber of radiant thermal energy?
questions.Explanation: A dull, matte black surface is both a good emitter and a good absorber of thermal radiation (approaching an ideal black body), while shiny polished surfaces are good reflectors.

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The greenhouse effect in Earth's atmosphere is primarily caused by:
questions.OptionA: Convection currents transporting warm oceanic air to the polar ice caps

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Newton's law of cooling is valid only under which condition?
questions.OptionA: The body is cooling inside a complete vacuum
questions.OptionB: Heat loss occurs strictly by radiation following the Stefan-Boltzmann law
questions.OptionC: The cooling substance undergoes a continuous phase transition
questions.OptionD: The temperature excess of the cooling body over its surroundings is relatively small

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A progressive wave has a frequency of 250 Hz and a wavelength of 1.4 m. Calculate its velocity of propagation.
questions.Explanation: Wave velocity v = f * λ = 250 Hz * 1.4 m = 350 m/s.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which of the following wave phenomena can ONLY be exhibited by transverse waves and NOT by longitudinal waves?
questions.Explanation: Polarization restricts the plane of particle vibration to a single plane perpendicular to wave propagation; longitudinal waves vibrate parallel to the direction of propagation and cannot be polarized.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The displacement y of a traveling wave is given by y = 0.05 sin(100π t - 2π x), where x and y are in meters and t is in seconds. What is the frequency of the wave?
questions.Explanation: Comparing with y = A sin(ωt - kx): angular frequency ω = 100π rad/s. Frequency f = ω / (2π) = 100π / (2π) = 50 Hz.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: From the equation y = 0.05 sin(100π t - 2π x), determine the wavelength of the wave.
questions.Explanation: Comparing with y = A sin(ωt - kx): wave number k = 2π / λ = 2π m^-1. Therefore, wavelength λ = 2π / (2π) = 1.0 m.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What is the distance between two consecutive nodes in a stationary (standing) wave of wavelength λ?
questions.Explanation: In a stationary wave, the distance between any two adjacent nodes (or two adjacent antinodes) is half a wavelength: λ / 2.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A wave of frequency 500 Hz travels with a speed of 340 m/s in air. What is the phase difference between two points along the wave separated by a distance of 0.17 m?
questions.Explanation: Wavelength λ = v / f = 340 / 500 = 0.68 m. Phase difference Δφ = (2π / λ) * Δx = (2π / 0.68) * 0.17 = 2π * 0.25 = π/2 radians (or 90°).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which of the following is a key distinguishing feature of a stationary (standing) wave compared to a progressive wave?
questions.OptionA: Standing waves have continuously traveling crests and troughs
questions.OptionB: All particles in a standing wave vibrate with the exact same amplitude
questions.OptionC: Standing waves do not transmit net energy through the medium
questions.OptionD: Standing waves can only be produced in an acoustic vacuum
questions.Option_a: Standing waves have continuously traveling crests and troughs
questions.Option_b: All particles in a standing wave vibrate with the exact same amplitude
questions.Option_c: Standing waves do not transmit net energy through the medium
questions.Option_d: Standing waves can only be produced in an acoustic vacuum
questions.Explanation: In a stationary wave, energy is confined between nodes; there is no net energy transport along the medium, unlike progressive waves which continuously transmit energy.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What is defined as a line or surface joining all points in a wave that vibrate in identical phase?
questions.Explanation: A wavefront is the locus of all adjacent points or particles in a wave medium that possess the same phase of vibration.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A water wave of wavelength 0.8 m travels from deep water into shallow water where its speed is reduced from 4.0 m/s to 2.5 m/s. What is its new wavelength?
questions.Explanation: Frequency remains unchanged across different media: f = v1 / λ1 = 4.0 / 0.8 = 5.0 Hz. In shallow water: λ2 = v2 / f = 2.5 / 5.0 = 0.50 m.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which type of wave requires a material medium to propagate?
questions.Explanation: Mechanical waves (sound waves, seismic waves, water ripples) require material particles to transmit vibrational energy, whereas electromagnetic waves propagate in a vacuum.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: When two identical progressive waves traveling in opposite directions along a string superimpose, what type of wave is formed?
questions.Explanation: Superposition of two waves of equal amplitude, frequency, and wavelength traveling in opposite directions produces a stationary (standing) wave.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: In a transverse wave traveling horizontally, the particles of the medium vibrate:
questions.OptionA: Parallel to the direction of wave propagation
questions.OptionC: In circles along the direction of propagation
questions.OptionD: Perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation
questions.Option_a: Parallel to the direction of wave propagation
questions.Option_c: In circles along the direction of propagation
questions.Option_d: Perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation
questions.Explanation: In transverse waves, particles vibrate at right angles (perpendicular) to the path of wave propagation.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The amplitude of a wave is doubled. By what factor does the energy carried by the wave increase?
questions.Explanation: The energy (and intensity) of a wave is directly proportional to the square of its amplitude (E ∝ A^2). Doubling A increases the energy by 2^2 = 4.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A sound wave of frequency 440 Hz travels in air at a speed of 330 m/s. Calculate its wavelength.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A ship's echo-sounder emits an ultrasonic pulse towards the seabed and receives the echo 1.2 seconds later. If the speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m/s, determine the depth of the sea.
questions.Explanation: Total travel distance 2d = v * t => d = (v * t) / 2 = (1500 * 1.2) / 2 = 1800 / 2 = 900 m.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The fundamental frequency of a closed organ pipe of length 0.85 m is 100 Hz. If the speed of sound in air is 340 m/s, what harmonic is represented if the pipe produces a note of 300 Hz?
questions.Explanation: A closed pipe produces only odd harmonics: f_n = n * f_1 (n = 1, 3, 5...). For f = 300 Hz = 3 * 100 Hz, it is the 3rd harmonic (which is the 1st overtone).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which subjective characteristic of a musical sound depends primarily on the number and relative intensities of overtones (harmonics) present?
questions.Explanation: The quality or timbre of a musical note depends on the wave waveform, which is determined by the presence and relative amplitudes of overtones accompanying the fundamental frequency.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded simultaneously. What is the beat frequency heard by a listener?
questions.Explanation: Beat frequency f_beat = |f1 - f2| = |260 - 256| = 4 Hz (4 beats per second).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A sonometer wire of length 0.50 m vibrates with a fundamental frequency of 200 Hz under a tension of 40 N. Calculate the mass per unit length (linear density) of the wire.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: In which medium does sound travel with the greatest velocity?
questions.Explanation: Sound speed depends on medium elasticity and density: v = sqrt(E / ρ). Solids like steel are much more elastic than liquids and gases, carrying sound at ~5000 m/s compared to 1500 m/s in water and 340 m/s in air (cannot travel in vacuum).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The fundamental frequency of an open organ pipe of length L is f_0. If one end is now closed, what is the new fundamental frequency of the closed pipe?
questions.Explanation: For an open pipe: f_open = v / (2L) = f_0. For a closed pipe of same length: f_closed = v / (4L) = f_0 / 2.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What phenomenon occurs when the frequency of an applied periodic force matches the natural frequency of an oscillating system, causing large amplitude vibrations?
questions.Explanation: Resonance occurs when a system is driven at its natural resonant frequency, maximizing energy transfer and producing maximum amplitude oscillations.

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.Explanation: Distance there and back 2d = 2 * 85 = 170 m. Time taken t = 2d / v = 170 / 340 = 0.50 s.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What acoustic effect describes the persistence of sound in an enclosed hall due to repeated reflections from walls and ceilings?
questions.Explanation: Reverberation is the prolonged persistence of sound within an auditorium caused by multiple overlapping reflections from boundary surfaces after the source has stopped.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Reflection of Light and Plane/Curved Mirrors
questions.Question: An object of height 4.0 cm is placed 20 cm in front of a concave mirror of radius of curvature 30 cm. Calculate the height of the image formed.

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.Question: A swimming pool of actual water depth 2.4 m appears shallower when viewed from directly above. If the refractive index of water is 1.33, calculate its apparent depth.

questions.Option_d: The eye lens loses its elasticity with aging

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which type of spectacle lens is used to correct myopia?
questions.Explanation: A diverging (concave) lens diverges incoming parallel rays slightly before entering the eye, enabling them to focus precisely on the retina.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) is corrected using which type of lens?
questions.Explanation: In hypermetropia, rays focus behind the retina; a converging (convex) lens adds refractive power to bring the focal point forward onto the retina.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: An astronomical telescope in normal adjustment consists of an objective lens of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. What is the magnifying power of the telescope?
questions.Explanation: In normal adjustment, angular magnification M = f_objective / f_eyepiece = 100 cm / 5 cm = 20.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What is the length of the telescope tube in the astronomical telescope described above (f_o = 100 cm, f_e = 5 cm) in normal adjustment?
questions.Explanation: In normal adjustment, the distance between objective and eyepiece is L = f_o + f_e = 100 + 5 = 105 cm.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: In a compound microscope, what are the characteristics of the intermediate image formed by the objective lens?
questions.Explanation: The objective lens of a compound microscope produces a real, inverted, and magnified intermediate image, which then falls within the focal length of the eyepiece lens.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What visual defect is caused by the gradual loss of accommodation of the crystalline lens in elderly persons?
questions.Explanation: Presbyopia is age-related hardening of the crystalline lens and weakening of ciliary muscles, making accommodation for near vision difficult.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which optical part of the human eye performs a role functionally equivalent to the photographic film or CCD sensor of a digital camera?
questions.Explanation: The retina is the light-sensitive surface containing photoreceptor cells (rods and cones) where real images are formed, analogous to the film or sensor in a camera.

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.OptionB: Provide nourishment to the vitreous humor

questions.Option_c: Regulate the amount of light entering the eye by controlling aperture size
questions.Option_d: Transmit electrical impulses to the brain
questions.Explanation: The iris acts like the diaphragm of a camera, expanding or constricting the pupil aperture to control the intensity of light entering the eye.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A short-sighted person cannot focus distinctly on objects situated further than 2.0 m from their eyes. Determine the focal length and power of the corrective lens required.
questions.Explanation: To see objects at infinity (u = ∞) clearly, the virtual image must be formed at the far point (v = -2.0 m): 1/f = 1/v - 1/u = -1/2.0 - 0 = -0.5 m^-1 => f = -2.0 m. Power P = 1 / f = -0.50 D.

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.OptionC: Hypermetropia; corrected with a converging lens
questions.Option_a: Astigmatism; corrected with a cylindrical lens
questions.Option_b: Myopia; corrected with a biconcave lens
questions.Option_c: Hypermetropia; corrected with a converging lens
questions.Explanation: Astigmatism is caused by non-uniform (aspherical) curvature of the cornea, focusing rays into lines rather than points, and is corrected with cylindrical lenses.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A simple magnifying glass has a focal length of 5.0 cm. What is its angular magnification when the image is formed at the near point of distinct vision (D = 25 cm)?
questions.Explanation: Magnification at near point: M = 1 + D / f = 1 + 25 / 5 = 1 + 5 = 6.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What is the speed of all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum?
questions.Explanation: All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light c ≈ 3.0 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which electromagnetic wave is primarily responsible for the production of vitamin D in human skin and can also cause sunburns?
questions.Explanation: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation triggers vitamin D synthesis in skin, but excessive exposure causes tanning, painful sunburns, and cellular DNA damage.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: In Young's double-slit experiment, what is the effect on the fringe separation (fringe width) if the distance between the slits is halved while keeping the slit-to-screen distance constant?
questions.Explanation: Fringe width w = (λ * D) / d. Since fringe width is inversely proportional to slit separation d, halving d doubles the fringe width.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which wave phenomenon proves conclusively that light waves are transverse rather than longitudinal?
questions.Explanation: Only transverse waves (where vibrations occur perpendicular to wave travel) can be polarized. Longitudinal waves cannot be polarized.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What type of electromagnetic radiation is emitted by warm objects and detected by thermal imaging cameras and night-vision equipment?
questions.Explanation: Infrared radiation is emitted by all warm objects as thermal radiation and is utilized in thermal night-vision scopes and TV remote controls.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: The bending of waves around the edges of an obstacle or through a narrow aperture is called:
questions.Explanation: Diffraction is the spreading or bending of wave crests around obstacles or corners when the obstacle size is comparable to the wavelength.

questions.OptionA: Sound waves are electromagnetic while light is mechanical

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which electromagnetic wave possesses the highest photon energy and highest penetrating power, originating from nuclear transitions?
questions.Explanation: Gamma rays have the highest frequencies, shortest wavelengths, and greatest photon energies (E = hf), originating from nuclear decay with immense penetrating power.

questions.Explanation: Light reflected horizontally from water or tarmac is partially polarized horizontally; Polaroid lenses with vertical transmission axes block this glare.

questions.Question: The electric potential at a distance r from an isolated point charge Q in free space is given by:
questions.Explanation: Electric potential V is a scalar quantity defined as work done per unit charge from infinity: V = Q / (4πε_0 r). (Contrast with field intensity E which varies as 1/r^2).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Two parallel metal plates separated by 4.0 mm have a potential difference of 120 V maintained between them. What is the magnitude of the uniform electric field between the plates?
questions.Explanation: Uniform field E = V / d = 120 V / (4.0 x 10^-3 m) = 30,000 V/m = 3.0 x 10^4 V/m (or N/C).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Two capacitors of 4 μF and 6 μF are connected in parallel across a 50 V source. What is the total electrical charge stored by the combination?
questions.Explanation: Equivalent parallel capacitance C_eq = 4 + 6 = 10 μF = 1.0 x 10^-5 F. Total charge Q = C_eq * V = 1.0 x 10^-5 F * 50 V = 5.0 x 10^-4 C (0.50 mC).

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.Question: What happens to the resistance of a uniform wire of resistance 8.0 Ω if it is stretched uniformly to twice its original length without altering its mass or density?

questions.OptionA: The potentiometer has zero electrical resistance along its wire
questions.OptionB: The potentiometer works equally well on alternating currents
questions.OptionC: The potentiometer draws no electric current from the cell at null balance point
questions.OptionD: The potentiometer amplifies small voltage signals

questions.Option_c: The potentiometer draws no electric current from the cell at null balance point
questions.Option_d: The potentiometer amplifies small voltage signals

questions.OptionB: The electromotive force of a circuit equals the product of current and total power

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Current Electricity, Resistance, and Ohm Law
questions.Question: Which of the following devices is a non-ohmic conductor?
questions.Explanation: A p-n junction semiconductor diode does not have a constant ratio of V/I (its I-V characteristic curve is non-linear), making it a non-ohmic device.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Current Electricity, Resistance, and Ohm Law
questions.Question: In a meter bridge experiment, a standard resistor of 3.0 Ω is placed in the right gap and an unknown resistor R is in the left gap. The balance point is obtained at 40 cm from the left end. What is the value of R?
questions.Explanation: Meter bridge balance condition: R / L1 = S / (100 - L1) => R / 40 = 3.0 / 60 => R = (3.0 * 40) / 60 = 120 / 60 = 2.0 Ω.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Current Electricity, Resistance, and Ohm Law
questions.Question: What happens to the electrical resistance of pure metallic conductors when their temperature increases?
questions.OptionA: Resistance decreases because more valence electrons are freed
questions.OptionB: Resistance stays constant because electron charge is invariant
questions.OptionC: Resistance increases due to increased lattice ion vibrations scattering conduction electrons
questions.Option_a: Resistance decreases because more valence electrons are freed
questions.Option_b: Resistance stays constant because electron charge is invariant
questions.Option_c: Resistance increases due to increased lattice ion vibrations scattering conduction electrons
questions.Explanation: In metals, heating increases the amplitude of thermal vibrations of positive metal ions in the lattice, increasing the collision rate and scattering of conduction electrons, which increases resistance.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Current Electricity, Resistance, and Ohm Law
questions.Question: Kirchhoff's first law (the junction rule), stating that total current entering a junction equals total current leaving it, is a direct consequence of:
questions.Explanation: Kirchhoff's current law (KCL, ΣI = 0) reflects the fundamental principle of conservation of electric charge: charge cannot accumulate or disappear at a circuit junction.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Current Electricity, Resistance, and Ohm Law
questions.Question: Kirchhoff's second law (the loop rule), stating that the algebraic sum of emfs around any closed loop equals the algebraic sum of IR drops, is a consequence of:
questions.Explanation: Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL, ΣE = ΣIR) is based on the principle of conservation of energy: the work done per unit charge around any closed path in an electrostatic field is zero.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Current Electricity, Resistance, and Ohm Law
questions.Question: Four identical cells, each of emf 2.0 V and internal resistance 0.4 Ω, are connected in parallel. What is the effective emf and internal resistance of the combination?
questions.Explanation: Identical cells in parallel produce an effective emf equal to that of a single cell (2.0 V), while their internal resistances combine in parallel: r_eff = r / n = 0.4 / 4 = 0.1 Ω.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Electrical Energy, Heating Effect, and Metering
questions.Question: An electric immersion heater rated 2000 W, 240 V is used for 3 hours daily for 30 days. Calculate the electrical energy consumed in kilowatt-hours (kWh).
questions.Explanation: Power in kW = 2000 W / 1000 = 2 kW. Total hours t = 3 h/day * 30 days = 90 hours. Energy = Power * time = 2 kW * 90 h = 180 kWh.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Electrical Energy, Heating Effect, and Metering
questions.Question: If the cost of electrical energy is 25 Naira per kWh, calculate the monthly electricity bill for operating the 2000 W heater described above (consuming 180 kWh).
questions.Explanation: Cost = Energy (kWh) * Rate = 180 kWh * 25 Naira/kWh = 4,500 Naira.

questions.OptionC: Connecting a capacitor in series with the galvanometer coil

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Electrical Energy, Heating Effect, and Metering
questions.Question: A galvanometer has an internal resistance of 20 Ω and gives full-scale deflection with a current of 10 mA. Calculate the shunt resistance required to convert it into an ammeter reading up to 5.0 A.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Topic: Electrical Energy, Heating Effect, and Metering
questions.Question: A galvanometer has an internal resistance of 50 Ω and full-scale deflection current of 2.0 mA. Determine the series multiplier resistance needed to convert it into a voltmeter reading up to 10 V.

questions.Question: Which wire in a standard 3-pin plug is a safety feature that connects the metal chassis of an electrical appliance to the ground?
questions.Explanation: The earth wire connects the external metal casing of appliances to ground. If a fault causes the live wire to touch the chassis, fault current surges to earth, blowing the fuse and preventing electric shock.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which radiation detector relies on ionization of low-pressure argon gas producing an avalanche pulse of current between an anode wire and cathode cylinder?
questions.Explanation: A Geiger-Muller tube uses high electric field between a central wire anode and cylindrical metal cathode to amplify ionizing events in low-pressure noble gas into detectable electrical pulses.

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.OptionA: Alpha particles travel at the speed of light
questions.OptionB: Alpha particles have a double positive charge (+2e) and move relatively slowly with large mass, exerting strong electrostatic forces on orbital electrons
questions.OptionC: Alpha particles carry negative charges that neutralize atomic nuclei
questions.OptionD: Alpha particles induce immediate nuclear fission in air molecules

questions.Option_d: Alpha particles induce immediate nuclear fission in air molecules
questions.Explanation: Alpha particles have +2e charge and large mass, moving slower than electrons. Their intense electrostatic field strongly strips electrons from gas molecules, giving them exceptionally high specific ionization.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A radiation counter records a background count of 20 counts per minute. When a radioactive source is placed near, the total count rate is 260 counts per minute. What will the corrected source count rate be after 3 half-lives?
questions.Explanation: Initial corrected count rate = 260 - 20 = 240 cpm. After 3 half-lives: 240 / (2^3) = 240 / 8 = 30 counts per minute.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What happens to a radioactive nucleus when it emits a gamma ray photon?

questions.Option_c: It transforms into an isobar of itself
questions.Option_d: It drops from an excited nuclear energy state to a lower or ground state with no change in mass number or atomic number
questions.Explanation: Gamma emission is a purely electromagnetic transition where an excited nucleus de-excites to a lower energy state. Neither A nor Z changes.

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which radioisotope is widely utilized in medical radiography and radiotherapy for destroying cancerous tumors?
questions.Explanation: Cobalt-60 emits high-energy penetrating gamma rays used in external beam radiotherapy to sterilize surgical instruments and destroy malignant cancer cells.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What is the phenomenon called when a heavy atomic nucleus such as uranium-235 splits into two lighter fragments upon absorbing a slow thermal neutron?
questions.Explanation: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy, unstable nucleus (such as U-235 or Pu-239) into two medium-sized daughter nuclei accompanied by prompt neutrons and tremendous energy release.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: In a nuclear power reactor, what is the specific role of the moderator (such as heavy water or pure graphite)?
questions.OptionA: To absorb all excess neutrons and shut down the reactor
questions.OptionB: To cool the outer containment dome
questions.OptionC: To shield workers from escaping gamma radiation
questions.OptionD: To slow down energetic fast fission neutrons so they can be readily captured by uranium-235 nuclei

questions.Explanation: Fast neutrons emitted in fission are inefficient at causing further fission. Moderators collide elastically with fast neutrons to slow them to thermal velocities where U-235 absorption cross-section is high.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What material is commonly used in nuclear reactor control rods to regulate or halt the fission chain reaction?
questions.Explanation: Boron and cadmium have very high neutron capture cross-sections without undergoing fission, allowing them to absorb excess neutrons and regulate chain reaction rates.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What is nuclear fusion?
questions.OptionA: The splitting of a massive nucleus into two fragments
questions.OptionB: The emission of beta particles from an unstable isotope
questions.OptionC: The process where two light atomic nuclei combine at extremely high temperature and pressure to form a heavier nucleus
questions.OptionD: The spontaneous decay of a proton into a neutron

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What is the primary source of energy in the Sun and other stars?
questions.OptionA: Controlled nuclear fission of uranium and thorium

questions.Explanation: The sun is powered by thermonuclear fusion through the proton-proton chain reaction, where hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium at temperatures of tens of millions of Kelvin.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Why does nuclear fusion require extremely high temperatures on the order of 10^7 to 10^8 K to occur?
questions.OptionA: The fusing nuclei need massive kinetic energy to overcome mutual electrostatic (Coulomb) repulsion before the short-range strong nuclear force takes over
questions.OptionB: High temperature is needed to vaporize all nuclear matter into photons
questions.OptionC: Electrons must be stripped of all gravitational mass
questions.OptionD: High temperature increases the half-life of hydrogen isotopes

questions.Option_d: High temperature increases the half-life of hydrogen isotopes
questions.Explanation: Both positively charged nuclei strongly repel each other electrostatically. Only ultra-high thermal kinetic energies allow them to get close enough (10^-15 m) for attractive strong nuclear forces to bind them.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What is the binding energy of an atomic nucleus?
questions.OptionA: The gravitational energy holding the atom together

questions.OptionD: The kinetic energy of neutrons in the nucleus

questions.Option_c: The electrostatic energy binding orbital electrons to the nucleus
questions.Option_d: The kinetic energy of neutrons in the nucleus
questions.Explanation: Nuclear binding energy is the energy required to disassemble a nucleus into its constituent free protons and neutrons, equal to the mass defect converted to energy (Δm c^2).

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which nucleus has the highest binding energy per nucleon, representing the most stable atomic nucleus in nature?
questions.Explanation: Iron-56 (and nickel-62) sits at the peak of the binding energy per nucleon curve (~8.8 MeV per nucleon), making it the most tightly bound and energetically stable nucleus in nature.

questions.OptionD: The minimum mass of fissile material required to sustain a self-perpetuating chain reaction

questions.Option_d: The minimum mass of fissile material required to sustain a self-perpetuating chain reaction
questions.Explanation: Critical mass is the smallest amount of fissile isotope needed so that neutron losses by leakage or absorption do not prevent a self-sustaining continuous nuclear chain reaction.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: In the fission reaction ^235_92 U + ^1_0 n -> ^141_56 Ba + ^92_36 Kr + k ^1_0 n, determine the number of prompt neutrons k released.
questions.Explanation: Balancing mass numbers: 235 + 1 = 141 + 92 + k * 1 => 236 = 233 + k => k = 236 - 233 = 3 neutrons.

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.OptionA: The semiconductor has completely overlapping conduction and valence bands
questions.OptionB: The insulator contains millions of mobile holes in its conduction band
questions.OptionC: The semiconductor has a relatively narrow forbidden energy gap (~1.1 eV for silicon), allowing some electrons to thermally jump into the conduction band

questions.Option_d: The semiconductor has zero valence electrons in its outer shell
questions.Explanation: Semiconductors have narrow band gaps (~1 eV), permitting thermal excitation of valence electrons across the gap into the conduction band; insulators have wide forbidden gaps (> 5 eV).

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.OptionA: Doping pure silicon with a pentavalent impurity atom like phosphorus or arsenic
questions.OptionB: Heating pure silicon to its melting point in a vacuum
questions.OptionC: Irradiating pure silicon with gamma radiation
questions.OptionD: Doping pure silicon with a trivalent impurity atom like boron, aluminum, or indium

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What are the majority charge carriers in an n-type semiconductor?
questions.Explanation: Doping with pentavalent atoms (Group 15, e.g. phosphorus) provides extra unbonded electrons, making free electrons the majority carriers and holes the minority carriers.

questions.Subject: Physics

questions.OptionB: A narrow region near the junction devoid of mobile charge carriers, containing immobilized positive and negative donor/acceptor ions
questions.OptionC: A region filled with dense clouds of free electrons and holes
questions.OptionD: An insulating ceramic plate separating p and n regions

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What happens to the width of the depletion layer when a p-n junction diode is FORWARD BIASED?
questions.OptionA: The depletion layer widens and barrier potential increases

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: In full-wave rectification using a bridge rectifier, how many semiconductor diodes are connected in the bridge network?
questions.Explanation: A standard bridge rectifier circuit employs 4 diodes arranged in a closed bridge loop to convert both positive and negative alternating voltage half-cycles into pulsating direct current.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What is the primary function of a large electrolytic capacitor connected in parallel with the load in a DC power supply rectifier circuit?
questions.OptionA: Smoothing the pulsating direct current to produce a steady DC output voltage
questions.OptionB: Stepping down the mains alternating voltage
questions.OptionC: Preventing reverse bias voltage breakdown in the diodes
questions.Option_a: Smoothing the pulsating direct current to produce a steady DC output voltage
questions.Option_b: Stepping down the mains alternating voltage
questions.Option_c: Preventing reverse bias voltage breakdown in the diodes
questions.Explanation: A reservoir/smoothing capacitor charges to peak voltage and discharges gradually through the load during valley periods of the rectified wave, greatly reducing voltage ripple.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What happens to the electrical conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor when its temperature is increased?
questions.OptionA: Its conductivity decreases due to lattice vibration scattering
questions.OptionB: Its conductivity increases significantly because thermal energy breaks covalent bonds and creates more electron-hole pairs
questions.Option_a: Its conductivity decreases due to lattice vibration scattering
questions.Option_b: Its conductivity increases significantly because thermal energy breaks covalent bonds and creates more electron-hole pairs
questions.Explanation: Unlike metals, semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance. Heating liberates many more electron-hole charge carriers, causing conductivity to rise dramatically.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What type of optoelectronic semiconductor device emits visible light when forward biased due to radiative electron-hole recombination?
questions.Explanation: In a forward-biased LED, electrons injected from n-type recombine with holes from p-type near the junction, releasing energy as photons across the direct band gap.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: A Zener diode is specifically designed to operate in which operating region of its characteristic curve for voltage regulation?
questions.Explanation: A Zener diode operates in reverse bias at its characteristic Zener breakdown voltage (V_Z), maintaining a stable constant voltage across its terminals despite variations in supply voltage or load.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: What are the charge carriers responsible for electrical conduction in an intrinsic semiconductor?
questions.OptionA: Both free electrons and positive holes in equal numbers
questions.Option_a: Both free electrons and positive holes in equal numbers
questions.Explanation: In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor, thermal excitation generates equal numbers of free conduction band electrons and valence band holes (n_e = n_h = n_i), both contributing to conduction.

questions.Subject: Physics
questions.Question: Which electronic component can act as an electronic switch and an electrical signal amplifier in solid-state circuits?
questions.Explanation: A transistor (such as an npn or pnp BJT) uses a small base current to control a much larger collector current, functioning both as an amplifier and as a high-speed electronic switch.
